screens.title: Ansible fundamentals: agentless and declarative
screens.narratorSegment: Start by anchoring the two defining properties of Ansible for network automation: agentless execution and a declarative model. Agentless means you do not install persistent software on routers or switches. Instead, Ansible connects over SSH or the platform's supported protocol and executes modules remotely. For network teams this reduces management overhead because you maintain automation tools only on the control node. Declarative means you describe the desired device state rather than the exact procedural steps to reach it. For example, you declare that VLAN 200 should exist with a specific name, and Ansible, using a module like ios_config, ensures the device matches that state. A clear benefit of declarative automation is idempotency: running the same playbook repeatedly results in no additional changes when the device already matches the desired state. A common misconception is that declarative means Ansible magically figures out complex rollbacks; in reality you still define specific desired states and need to plan for removal or rollbacks explicitly. Practice thinking in terms of desired state for each task: what should the running configuration look like after the playbook completes? That shift in mindset reduces fragile procedural scripts and leads to repeatable, safer automation. How would you express a current manual configuration task as a desired state instead of a sequence of commands?

keyIdea.text: Agentless connects via SSH; declarative playbooks state the desired device configuration so automation is repeatable and idempotent.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Agentless & Declarative
Agentless design

Ansible communicates over SSH or WinRM and does not require an agent installed on managed nodes. For network devices this simplifies deployment and reduces ongoing upkeep.

Why it matters
  • Lower operational overhead: only the control node needs Ansible installed.
  • Easier adoption across heterogeneous devices that support standard protocols.
  • Fewer software updates and fewer security surfaces on devices.
Analogy

Think of Ansible as a remote technician who connects with a secure session instead of permanently installing a helper on every device.

Declarative playbooks

Write YAML describing the desired state of devices. Ansible modules evaluate current state and apply only needed changes, enabling idempotent operations.

Example: VLAN
Declare VLAN 200 with a name. If it already exists, the module reports ok rather than changing it again.
Common misconception
Declarative doesn't remove unintended state automatically; you must declare the correct desired end state including removals if needed.
Key takeaway
Think desired state first. Use agentless connections and idempotent modules to make automation safe and repeatable.

screens.title: Ansible architecture explained
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the architecture clarifies who runs what and where state is evaluated. The control node is the machine where you install Ansible and execute playbooks. It orchestrates connections and pushes modules or executes them over network sessions. Managed nodes are the routers and switches you control; Ansible connects to them using SSH and makes configuration changes. The inventory is the authoritative list that maps group names to host aliases and supplies connection variables like ansible_host, ansible_user, ansible_password, and ansible_network_os. Modules are the units of work; network modules such as ios_config and ios_command encapsulate device-specific tasks and are written to be idempotent. Playbooks glue tasks together — they declare hosts to target, gather_facts (often disabled for network devices), and a list of tasks. A frequent troubleshooting step is verifying that the inventory variables match the device's expected login credentials and network OS. A misconception is to treat the inventory as only a flat host list; in reality you can group hosts and set group-level variables for cleaner, reusable targeting. When you design automation, think about where variables belong: host, group, or all:vars to avoid accidental overrides.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Ansible Architecture
Architecture components
Control Node
Where Ansible runs and holds playbooks. Typically a Linux VM or workstation.
Managed Nodes
Routers and switches that Ansible connects to, typically over SSH for network devices.
Inventory
Lists hosts and variables like ansible_host and ansible_network_os to direct playbooks correctly.
Modules & Playbooks
Modules do the work; playbooks sequence tasks and express the desired state in YAML.
Key takeaway

Structure your inventory and variables deliberately so playbooks target groups reliably and avoid credential mismatches.

Practical example
Group: cisco_ios_xe — hosts: iosxe_router1, iosxe_switch1 — host vars: ansible_host, ansible_user, ansible_password, ansible_network_os=ios — all:vars: ansible_connection=network_cli, ansible_become=yes
Common mistake
Putting credentials in many places causes maintenance headaches; prefer group vars or Vault to centralize secrets.
Reflection
Which variables in your inventory should be host-specific and which can be group-level defaults?

screens.title: Inventory file example and variables
screens.narratorSegment: The inventory file is the map Ansible uses to find and connect to devices. In many network labs you'll use the INI format with groups and host variables. A practical inventory snippet for Cisco IOS XE devices shows a group named cisco_ios_xe with two hosts. Each host gets ansible_host, ansible_user, ansible_password, and ansible_network_os so modules behave correctly. At the group level we set ansible_connection to network_cli and enable privilege escalation with ansible_become and ansible_become_method. When you run playbooks, Ansible consults these variables to open an SSH session, optionally enter enable mode, and then run modules like ios_config. A common error is wrong variable names or typos — for example ansible_network_os must match module expectations. Another pitfall is storing passwords in plain text; prefer using Ansible Vault for production secrets. Use ansible-playbook with a syntax-check to catch YAML issues elsewhere, but inventory problems usually show as connection errors when you run your playbook. Practice: create a minimal inventory, run ping-like modules, and confirm the host resolves and accepts SSH before running configuration playbooks. Inventory file example and variables means inventory groups plus host and group variables direct connections and module behavior for cisco devices.. In practical terms, how to declare cisco ios xe hosts and connection settings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Inventory Example
Example inventory.ini
[cisco_ios_xe]
iosxe_router1 ansible_host=192.168.1.100 ansible_user=developer ansible_password=Cisco12345! ansible_network_os=ios
iosxe_switch1 ansible_host=192.168.1.101 ansible_user=developer ansible_password=Cisco12345! ansible_network_os=ios

[all:vars]
ansible_connection=network_cli
ansible_become=yes
ansible_become_method=enable
Notes
  • Group header defines a host set used by playbooks.
  • Host variables override group defaults for connection and credentials.
  • [all:vars] sets defaults like network_cli and enable escalation for every host.
Practical checklist
  1. Verify ansible_host resolves to the device IP address.
  2. Confirm ansible_user has correct privileges and ansible_become is set if enable is required.
  3. Move credentials to Vault for production to avoid plain text.
Common mistake

Typos in variable names or using the wrong connection type often cause SSH failures. Confirm variable names match module expectations.

screens.title: Playbook anatomy and YAML rules
screens.narratorSegment: Playbooks are YAML documents that list plays; each play targets hosts and defines tasks executed by modules. A minimal playbook begins with three dashes and includes a descriptive name, hosts, and gather_facts set to no for network devices to speed execution. Tasks are sequential entries with names and module invocations. For example, a banner configuration playbook uses cisco. ios. ios_config with lines and save_when parameters, registering the result to inspect later. YAML is indentation-sensitive: incorrect spaces will break parsing. Always use a consistent number of spaces per level and prefer two spaces. Use ansible-playbook --syntax-check to catch YAML structure issues before running. Another frequent error is quoting multi-line values incorrectly; when a module expects a list, provide lines: as a YAML sequence rather than a single combined string. Practice by copying the sample, running syntax-check, then executing in --check mode to preview changes. This workflow — write, syntax-check, dry-run, run — reduces accidental changes and helps you build confidence before touching production devices. When you register outputs, debug those variables to understand module responses and whether the module reported changed or ok.

keyIdea.text: Write YAML plays with clear hosts and tasks; always syntax-check and use check mode before applying changes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Playbook Anatomy
Example: configure_banner.yml
---
- name: Configure banner message on Cisco IOS XE devices
  hosts: cisco_ios_xe
  gather_facts: no

  tasks:
    - name: Set the login banner
      cisco.ios.ios_config:
        lines:
          - banner login ^CUnauthorized access is strictly prohibited.^C
        save_when: modified
      register: banner_result

    - name: Display banner configuration result
      debug:
        var: banner_result
Key points
  • Start with --- to mark YAML file start.
  • Use gather_facts: no for network devices to speed runs.
  • Register and debug module outputs to inspect changes reported.
YAML checklist
  • Use consistent indentation (prefer two spaces).
  • Lists must be YAML sequences; avoid inline comma-separated strings for module lists.
  • Run ansible-playbook --syntax-check before execution.
Pro tip

Use the editor's YAML mode to highlight indentation errors and save time troubleshooting.

screens.title: ios_config vs ios_command
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible provides network-focused modules with distinct purposes. The ios_config module is intended to change configuration: supply configuration lines or parents context, and optionally save when modified. It targets the device running configuration and aims to be idempotent. By contrast, ios_command runs arbitrary CLI show or operational commands and captures their output for verification. Use ios_command to validate a change or to gather information before making a decision in a playbook. For example, after using ios_config to create a VLAN, run ios_command with show vlan brief and inspect the returned stdout_lines to confirm the VLAN exists. A misconception is to use ios_command as a substitute for configuration; while ios_command can send configuration commands in some contexts, it is not designed for state-driven, idempotent configuration management. When building playbooks, adopt a pattern: change with ios_config, then verify with ios_command, register output, and debug or assert expected values. This separation keeps intent clear and simplifies reasoning about changed vs ok in execution reports. ios_config vs ios_command means ios_config for state changes; ios_command for read-only verification and output capture.. In practical terms, when to configure state vs when to run show commands. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › ios_config vs ios_command
ios_config (configuration)
Use to apply configuration lines; supports save_when to persist changes and is written to be idempotent.
  • Apply state: create VLANs, set banners, configure interfaces.
  • Idempotent modules avoid repeated changes when desired state exists.
  • Example option: save_when: modified to commit when changes occur.
ios_command (operational)
Run show commands or arbitrary CLI to gather output for verification or decision-making.
  • Use for validation: run show vlan brief after creating a VLAN.
  • Register stdout_lines to examine output programmatically.
  • Not intended for idempotent configuration tasks.
Pattern
Change with ios_config, verify with ios_command, register outputs, then assert or debug to confirm the desired state.
Key takeaway
Keep configuration and verification responsibilities separate for clarity.

screens.title: Run, verify, and interpret playbook output
screens.narratorSegment: When you run ansible-playbook you get structured output that tells you whether tasks changed devices or not. The key fields to watch are changed, ok, and failed. Changed indicates a module applied a modification; ok shows the module found the desired state already and did not change anything. For network engineers this is valuable: you can safely re-run playbooks and expect unchanged items to report ok. Before applying changes, always run ansible-playbook --syntax-check to validate the YAML structure and then run with --check --diff to perform a dry run. Check mode simulates changes and shows what would change without altering the device. Use the debug module and register to capture module results — inspecting the registered variable helps you understand whether a module found differences and why it reported changed. A common misconception is to trust only the top-level changed count; drilling into individual task output shows precisely which host and task made a change. After a successful run, you can run verification commands with ios_command to gather show output and cross-check the device state. Asking yourself why changed was true for a task helps avoid unintended configuration drift.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Run & Interpret
Run workflow
  1. ansible-playbook --syntax-check playbook.yml to validate YAML structure.
  2. ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini playbook.yml --check --diff to preview changes.
  3. Run the real playbook and inspect changed, ok, and failed counts for each host.
  4. Use ios_command to verify results when necessary.
Example
First run: changed=1 for VLAN creation. Second run: changed=0 because the device already matched the desired state.
Inspecting results
Register module outputs and use debug to print them. Look at stdout_lines for ios_command and at module-specific return values for ios_config to know what changed.
Common pitfall
Relying only on top-level changed counts may hide which task on which host made the change. Inspect per-task, per-host output.

screens.title: Idempotency in practice
screens.narratorSegment: Idempotency is central to configuration management: an idempotent operation leaves the system in the same final state no matter how many times it runs. In Ansible this means modules like ios_config are written to detect the current device state and only perform changes when necessary. For example, if your playbook creates VLAN 200 and assigns it a name, the first run may report changed, but subsequent runs should show ok because the configuration already matches the declared state. This property lets you schedule automation or re-run playbooks without fear of accumulating duplicate entries or repeated side effects. A common misconception is that idempotency replaces the need for testing; it does not. You still need to verify that the module's interpretation of current state matches your intent — sometimes device command output or parsing differences can lead to unexpected changes. Another practical note: idempotency depends on using supported modules and supplying configuration in the form the module expects. If you send raw unstructured commands instead of module parameters, you may lose idempotency. Practice by running a playbook twice, observing changed counts, and then examining registered variables to confirm why the second run reported ok.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Idempotency
What idempotency means

An operation is idempotent if executing it multiple times yields the same final state as executing it once. For network configuration, this prevents duplicate or unwanted changes from repeated automation runs.

Concrete example
Create VLAN 200 once. First run: changed. Second run: ok. The device remains in the intended state.
Misconception
Idempotency is not automatic for arbitrary CLI strings; use modules designed for state to preserve idempotency.
Check

After applying a change, run the playbook again and verify changed becomes zero. If not, inspect module returns and device state for discrepancies.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › VLAN Lab Walkthrough
inventory.ini (example)
[cisco_ios_xe]
my_cisco_device ansible_host=YOUR_DEVICE_IP ansible_user=developer ansible_password=Cisco12345! ansible_network_os=ios

[all:vars]
ansible_connection=network_cli
ansible_become=yes
ansible_become_method=enable
configure_vlan.yml (example)
---
- name: Configure a new VLAN on Cisco IOS XE device
  hosts: cisco_ios_xe
  gather_facts: no

  tasks:
    - name: Create VLAN 200 with name "Automation_VLAN"
      cisco.ios.ios_config:
        lines:
          - vlan 200
          - name Automation_VLAN
        parents: "vlan database"
        save_when: modified
      register: vlan_creation_result

    - name: Verify VLAN configuration
      cisco.ios.ios_command:
        commands: "show vlan brief"
      register: vlan_verify_output

    - name: Print VLAN verification output
      debug:
        var: vlan_verify_output.stdout_lines
Run checklist
  • Replace YOUR_DEVICE_IP and secure passwords with Vault for production.
  • ansible-playbook --syntax-check configure_vlan.yml
  • ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini configure_vlan.yml --check --diff
  • Then run: ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini configure_vlan.yml
Expected result
First run: VLAN created (changed). Second run: no change for VLAN (ok) demonstrating idempotency.

screens.title: Troubleshooting common Ansible issues
screens.narratorSegment: Common issues fall into a few predictable categories: YAML syntax and indentation, inventory mistakes, and connectivity or credential problems. YAML errors often manifest as parsing failures; use ansible-playbook --syntax-check to catch those before execution. Inventory mistakes, such as wrong host aliases or missing ansible_host variables, typically show as connection errors when the playbook runs. Verify that ansible_connection is set to network_cli for Cisco devices and that ansible_become is configured if enable mode is required. Connectivity errors may be due to SSH reachability, incorrect usernames, or privilege levels. A recurring security mistake is storing passwords in plain text in inventory files; for production, use Ansible Vault to encrypt sensitive data. Another helpful tactic is adding debug tasks to your playbook and registering module outputs: registered variables reveal parsing results and module return values that explain whether a change occurred. Finally, when you see unexpected changes on repeated runs, inspect whether the module's representation of current state matches the device's CLI behavior — differences in vendor output or module parsing can cause surprising results. Use dry runs and small incremental changes to isolate problems safely.

screens.title: Operational best practices for network automation
screens.narratorSegment: Adopt a few simple patterns to make Ansible automation robust and maintainable. First, organize variables: put common settings in group vars, reserve host vars for exceptions, and avoid scattering credentials across many files. Second, use Ansible Vault for secrets to avoid plaintext exposure. Third, prefer small, focused playbooks that do one thing well — it is easier to test and reason about a playbook that creates VLANs than a monolithic playbook that does many unrelated tasks. Fourth, always include verification steps: after changing state with ios_config, run ios_command to capture show output and assert or debug expected lines. Fifth, use syntax-check and check mode as part of your workflow. A typical practice is to run the playbook in CI or a controlled lab environment before deploying to production. Finally, register outputs and write small assertions if a module returns unexpected values. These habits reduce configuration drift, speed debugging, and increase confidence in automation. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how Ansible simplifies network configuration by using an agentless, declarative approach. We start with the architecture — control node, managed nodes, inventory and playbooks — and then move to practical files and examples you can run against Cisco IOS XE devices. You'll see how Ansible modules such as ios_config and ios_command let you apply and verify configuration, and why idempotency is essential so repeated runs are safe. We'll also walk through an inventory example and a small playbook that configures a login banner, then expand into a hands-on VLAN configuration activity. Understanding these pieces matters because they let you automate repetitive tasks reliably and reduce configuration drift. A common pitfall is YAML indentation or exposing credentials; we cover syntax checks and Ansible Vault for protecting secrets. By the end, you will be able to create a basic inventory, author a simple playbook, run a check mode dry run, and reason about why a module reports changed or ok. As you proceed, think about which manual router tasks you perform frequently and how a repeatable, idempotent playbook would save time and reduce risk.

These objectives map to concrete network automation skills you will practice in this lesson. First, you'll describe Ansible's architecture and core components so you can explain how control nodes and managed nodes interact. Second, you'll create and manage an inventory file to declare devices, grouping and assigning connection variables; this lets you target Cisco IOS XE devices reliably. Third, you will author basic YAML playbooks that use network modules to apply configuration on devices like configuring a login banner or creating a VLAN. Finally, you will understand and demonstrate idempotency: running a playbook repeatedly should not produce unintended changes. Each objective matters: architecture knowledge reduces troubleshooting time, a correct inventory prevents targeting the wrong devices, clear playbooks reduce human errors, and idempotency ensures safe repeatability. As you work through the lab, keep these objectives in mind and try to explain, in your own words, why each objective reduces operational risk.

This objective set prepares you for the lab: create an inventory, write a playbook that configures a VLAN, run it against a Cisco IOS XE device, and verify results. You'll practice a dry run using check mode and learn to interpret output fields like changed, ok, and failed. A concrete example: you'll author a playbook that creates VLAN 200 and names it Automation_VLAN, then use ios_command to run show vlan brief and validate the change. The lab intentionally includes debug and register tasks so you can inspect module output. Why this matters: being able to run a safe dry run and verify output reduces risk in production, and knowing how to inspect registered variables helps diagnose why a task didn't run or reported changed. During the exercise, notice common mistakes such as YAML indentation or storing plaintext passwords. We'll show how to use Ansible Vault to protect secrets. Aim to run the playbook twice and observe the changed count drop to zero — that's idempotency in practice.

Start by anchoring the two defining properties of Ansible for network automation: agentless execution and a declarative model. Agentless means you do not install persistent software on routers or switches. Instead, Ansible connects over SSH or the platform's supported protocol and executes modules remotely. For network teams this reduces management overhead because you maintain automation tools only on the control node. Declarative means you describe the desired device state rather than the exact procedural steps to reach it. For example, you declare that VLAN 200 should exist with a specific name, and Ansible, using a module like ios_config, ensures the device matches that state. A clear benefit of declarative automation is idempotency: running the same playbook repeatedly results in no additional changes when the device already matches the desired state. A common misconception is that declarative means Ansible magically figures out complex rollbacks; in reality you still define specific desired states and need to plan for removal or rollbacks explicitly. Practice thinking in terms of desired state for each task: what should the running configuration look like after the playbook completes? That shift in mindset reduces fragile procedural scripts and leads to repeatable, safer automation. How would you express a current manual configuration task as a desired state instead of a sequence of commands?

Understanding the architecture clarifies who runs what and where state is evaluated. The control node is the machine where you install Ansible and execute playbooks. It orchestrates connections and pushes modules or executes them over network sessions. Managed nodes are the routers and switches you control; Ansible connects to them using SSH and makes configuration changes. The inventory is the authoritative list that maps group names to host aliases and supplies connection variables like ansible_host, ansible_user, ansible_password, and ansible_network_os. Modules are the units of work; network modules such as ios_config and ios_command encapsulate device-specific tasks and are written to be idempotent. Playbooks glue tasks together — they declare hosts to target, gather_facts (often disabled for network devices), and a list of tasks. A frequent troubleshooting step is verifying that the inventory variables match the device's expected login credentials and network OS. A misconception is to treat the inventory as only a flat host list; in reality you can group hosts and set group-level variables for cleaner, reusable targeting. When you design automation, think about where variables belong: host, group, or all:vars to avoid accidental overrides.

The inventory file is the map Ansible uses to find and connect to devices. In many network labs you'll use the INI format with groups and host variables. A practical inventory snippet for Cisco IOS XE devices shows a group named cisco_ios_xe with two hosts. Each host gets ansible_host, ansible_user, ansible_password, and ansible_network_os so modules behave correctly. At the group level we set ansible_connection to network_cli and enable privilege escalation with ansible_become and ansible_become_method. When you run playbooks, Ansible consults these variables to open an SSH session, optionally enter enable mode, and then run modules like ios_config. A common error is wrong variable names or typos — for example ansible_network_os must match module expectations. Another pitfall is storing passwords in plain text; prefer using Ansible Vault for production secrets. Use ansible-playbook with a syntax-check to catch YAML issues elsewhere, but inventory problems usually show as connection errors when you run your playbook. Practice: create a minimal inventory, run ping-like modules, and confirm the host resolves and accepts SSH before running configuration playbooks. Inventory file example and variables means inventory groups plus host and group variables direct connections and module behavior for cisco devices.. In practical terms, how to declare cisco ios xe hosts and connection settings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Playbooks are YAML documents that list plays; each play targets hosts and defines tasks executed by modules. A minimal playbook begins with three dashes and includes a descriptive name, hosts, and gather_facts set to no for network devices to speed execution. Tasks are sequential entries with names and module invocations. For example, a banner configuration playbook uses cisco. ios. ios_config with lines and save_when parameters, registering the result to inspect later. YAML is indentation-sensitive: incorrect spaces will break parsing. Always use a consistent number of spaces per level and prefer two spaces. Use ansible-playbook --syntax-check to catch YAML structure issues before running. Another frequent error is quoting multi-line values incorrectly; when a module expects a list, provide lines: as a YAML sequence rather than a single combined string. Practice by copying the sample, running syntax-check, then executing in --check mode to preview changes. This workflow — write, syntax-check, dry-run, run — reduces accidental changes and helps you build confidence before touching production devices. When you register outputs, debug those variables to understand module responses and whether the module reported changed or ok.

Ansible provides network-focused modules with distinct purposes. The ios_config module is intended to change configuration: supply configuration lines or parents context, and optionally save when modified. It targets the device running configuration and aims to be idempotent. By contrast, ios_command runs arbitrary CLI show or operational commands and captures their output for verification. Use ios_command to validate a change or to gather information before making a decision in a playbook. For example, after using ios_config to create a VLAN, run ios_command with show vlan brief and inspect the returned stdout_lines to confirm the VLAN exists. A misconception is to use ios_command as a substitute for configuration; while ios_command can send configuration commands in some contexts, it is not designed for state-driven, idempotent configuration management. When building playbooks, adopt a pattern: change with ios_config, then verify with ios_command, register output, and debug or assert expected values. When you run ansible-playbook you get structured output that tells you whether tasks changed devices or not. The key fields to watch are changed, ok, and failed. Changed indicates a module applied a modification; ok shows the module found the desired state already and did not change anything. For network engineers this is valuable: you can safely re-run playbooks and expect unchanged items to report ok. Before applying changes, always run ansible-playbook --syntax-check to validate the YAML structure and then run with --check --diff to perform a dry run. Check mode simulates changes and shows what would change without altering the device. Use the debug module and register to capture module results — inspecting the registered variable helps you understand whether a module found differences and why it reported changed. A common misconception is to trust only the top-level changed count; drilling into individual task output shows precisely which host and task made a change. After a successful run, you can run verification commands with ios_command to gather show output and cross-check the device state. Asking yourself why changed was true for a task helps avoid unintended configuration drift.

Idempotency is central to configuration management: an idempotent operation leaves the system in the same final state no matter how many times it runs. In Ansible this means modules like ios_config are written to detect the current device state and only perform changes when necessary. For example, if your playbook creates VLAN 200 and assigns it a name, the first run may report changed, but subsequent runs should show ok because the configuration already matches the declared state. This property lets you schedule automation or re-run playbooks without fear of accumulating duplicate entries or repeated side effects. A common misconception is that idempotency replaces the need for testing; it does not. You still need to verify that the module's interpretation of current state matches your intent — sometimes device command output or parsing differences can lead to unexpected changes. Another practical note: idempotency depends on using supported modules and supplying configuration in the form the module expects. If you send raw unstructured commands instead of module parameters, you may lose idempotency. Practice by running a playbook twice, observing changed counts, and then examining registered variables to confirm why the second run reported ok.

Common issues fall into a few predictable categories: YAML syntax and indentation, inventory mistakes, and connectivity or credential problems. YAML errors often manifest as parsing failures; use ansible-playbook --syntax-check to catch those before execution. Inventory mistakes, such as wrong host aliases or missing ansible_host variables, typically show as connection errors when the playbook runs. Verify that ansible_connection is set to network_cli for Cisco devices and that ansible_become is configured if enable mode is required. Connectivity errors may be due to SSH reachability, incorrect usernames, or privilege levels. A recurring security mistake is storing passwords in plain text in inventory files; for production, use Ansible Vault to encrypt sensitive data. Another helpful tactic is adding debug tasks to your playbook and registering module outputs: registered variables reveal parsing results and module return values that explain whether a change occurred. Finally, when you see unexpected changes on repeated runs, inspect whether the module's representation of current state matches the device's CLI behavior — differences in vendor output or module parsing can cause surprising results. Use dry runs and small incremental changes to isolate problems safely.

Adopt a few simple patterns to make Ansible automation robust and maintainable. First, organize variables: put common settings in group vars, reserve host vars for exceptions, and avoid scattering credentials across many files. Second, use Ansible Vault for secrets to avoid plaintext exposure. Third, prefer small, focused playbooks that do one thing well — it is easier to test and reason about a playbook that creates VLANs than a monolithic playbook that does many unrelated tasks. Fourth, always include verification steps: after changing state with ios_config, run ios_command to capture show output and assert or debug expected lines. Fifth, use syntax-check and check mode as part of your workflow. A typical practice is to run the playbook in CI or a controlled lab environment before deploying to production. Finally, register outputs and write small assertions if a module returns unexpected values. These habits reduce configuration drift, speed debugging, and increase confidence in automation. The answer is idempotency: the first run made changes, the second found the desired state and did nothing. Let's recap the essential concepts to retain. First, Ansible is agentless and declarative: you describe the desired state and Ansible connects over SSH to achieve it. Second, the architecture revolves around a control node, managed nodes, inventory files, modules, and playbooks — organize variables carefully and use group-level defaults when appropriate. Third, use network modules such as ios_config for state changes and ios_command to verify outputs; register and debug module returns to understand behavior. Fourth, idempotency ensures that running a playbook repeatedly is safe; watch changed versus ok to confirm whether tasks actually modified devices. Finally, protect secrets with Ansible Vault, use syntax-check and check mode for safer runs, and keep playbooks focused for easier testing. These ideas together let you automate network tasks reliably while minimizing risk. As you continue practicing, aim to convert one manual, repetitive configuration into a small idempotent playbook and observe the changed counts across repeated runs.

Keep three concise reminders at your workspace. First, write declarative playbooks and prefer idempotent network modules to avoid repeated unintended changes. Second, structure your inventory and variables so playbooks target devices with the right connection settings and credentials, and protect those credentials with Ansible Vault. Third, adopt a safe workflow: syntax-check, dry-run with check and diff, run, verify with show commands, and re-run to confirm changed counts are zero. These practices keep automation predictable and make debugging faster. When you next automate a task, use this checklist as a preflight to reduce surprises and to make automation part of daily operations rather than a high-risk one-off.
